newsitem.title: USA: Jury begins deliberations in key tobacco trial.
newsitem.headline: Jury begins deliberations in key tobacco trial.

text.p: After nearly four weeks of testimony and five hours of closing arguments, jurors hearing a wrongful death lawsuit against R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co. began deliberating Friday on whether the company was negligent and caused the death of a smoker.
In a courthouse crowded with tobacco litigators, stock analysts and journalists, attorneys for Reynolds and plaintiff Dana Raulerson made their final pitches to the five-woman, one-man jury.

Raulerson sued Reynolds for the wrongful death of her sister, Jean Connor, a heavy smoker who took up the habit in her teens and smoked three packs a day until shortly before her death from lung cancer in October 1995. She was 49.

The jury was asked to decide whether Reynolds was negligent and made a defective and dangerous product that caused Connor's death. The jury recessed for the weekend after two hours of deliberations and was to resume its work on Monday.

Raulerson's attorney, Norwood "Woody" Wilner, who last summer won a landmark $750,000 judgment in a product liability trial against Brown & Williamson Tobacco Corp., said Connor was not a saint but declared Reynolds could not escape some responsibility for her death.

"Who made it cool to smoke poison?" Wilner asked the panel in a 58-minute closing statement. "Reynolds should not be able to say, 'It's all your fault, it's all your fault. We don't have any responsibility.'"

While some industry analysts have said a victory for Wilner in the Raulerson case could establish a trend against tobacco companies, others say the trial is dwarfed by ongoing talks between the industry and state attorneys general to settle a series of state Medicaid lawsuits.
"It's a little fight in a much bigger battle," said Martin Feldman, a tobacco analyst for Smith Barney who has watched much of the trial.

Last August, a Jacksonville jury awarded smoker Grady Carter and his wife $750,000 in a product liability case. The judgment against Brown & Williamson, a unit of Britain's B.A.T Industries Plc, was only the second monetary award against a tobacco company.
The industry called the judgment an aberration, and the case is under appeal.
"If you have a second win, it's much harder to argue that it's an aberration," Feldman said.
Wilner asked jurors to punish Reynolds for selling a dangerous product by awarding punitive damages. It is the first time a Florida jury has been asked to award such damages.
"We're asking you to send a message in this case. We're asking you to send a message to R.J. Reynolds, and many people will hear that message."

But R.J. Reynolds attorney Paul Crist said smoking was a lifestyle choice that Jean Connor made despite "vast" public knowledge about the health risks of smoking and told jurors the trial was an inappropriate place to send a message.
"The evidence is absolutely overwhelming that there was vast, widespread, unprecedented knowledge in the public domain about the health risks of smoking," he said.
Raulerson's lawyers did not ask jurors for a specific amount in punitive damages, saying only that they valued the loss to Connor's estate of her premature death at $250,000 to $300,000.
But Wilner's co-counsel, Ron Motley, noted the company's net worth was $2.769 billion.
"I think the evidence in this case justifies an award ... multiples in excess of whatever you award in actual damages," Motley said. "Would a million dollars punish them? What's going to stop them?"
Wilner, in his rebuttal to Crist's closing argument, said Reynolds had taken the unusual position of selling dangerous products and then suggesting people should not have bought them.
Reynolds "sells candy with razor blades inside to anyone who wants to buy ... then suggests that they shouldn't have bought that candy," he said. (
